summary: Specifies how IS-IS is extended to support Generalized Multi-Protocol Label Switching, including the encodings for advertising link information needed by GMPLS. It builds on the IS-IS traffic engineering extensions. It replaced RFC 4205 and has been updated by several later documents.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5307 adds fields that let IS-IS advertise properties of links used by GMPLS. Routers can learn link identifiers, switching capabilities, protection options, and which links may fail together.

what is link protection type in is-is
subtitle: IS-IS link advertisements for GMPLS switching, protection, and shared-risk information.

tldr.problem: GMPLS needs link properties for planning paths across packet, time-division, wavelength, and fiber switching links, but basic IS-IS traffic-engineering advertisements do not carry all of them.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds three sub-TLVs to the extended IS reachability TLV and adds the GMPLS-SRLG TLV for links that share a risk of failure.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5307 obsoletes RFC 4205, updates RFC 5305, and has been updated by RFC 6001, RFC 6002, and RFC 7074.

today: RFC 5307 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 4205 and updates RFC 5305. It has been updated by RFC 6001, RFC 6002, and RFC 7074.

sections.title: What IS-IS Advertises for GMPLS
sections.content:
Generalized Multi-Protocol Label Switching (GMPLS) uses links with different switching capabilities, including packet, time-division, wavelength, and fiber switching. RFC 5307 specifies how IS-IS carries the link-state information needed for GMPLS traffic engineering. It defines encodings that extend the IS-IS extended IS reachability TLV described by RFC 5305.

The RFC adds sub-TLVs for link identifiers, link protection type, and interface switching capability. It also adds the GMPLS Shared Risk Link Group (SRLG) TLV, which identifies links that may be affected by a shared failure source.
sections.plainLanguage: GMPLS needs more detail about links than ordinary packet routing needs. These IS-IS extensions let routers share that extra link information.

sections.title: Identifiers for Unnumbered Links
sections.content:
The Link Local/Remote Identifiers sub-TLV has type 4 and an 8-octet value. It contains a 4-octet local identifier followed by a 4-octet remote identifier. When the remote identifier is unknown, it is zero. These identifiers describe links that do not have IP addresses.

This sub-TLV must not appear more than once in an extended IS reachability TLV. If it appears more than once, a receiver should ignore all copies. The identifiers are exchanged in the Extended Local Circuit ID field of the IS-IS point-to-point three-way adjacency option.
sections.plainLanguage: For a link without IP addresses, each end can use a local identifier to describe it. The two identifiers appear together so routers can refer to the same link.

sections.title: Link Protection Information
sections.content:
The Link Protection Type sub-TLV has type 20 and is 2 octets long. Its first octet is a bit vector describing the link's protection capabilities, including shared and dedicated protection. The second octet is reserved: senders should set it to zero and receivers should ignore it.

This sub-TLV must not appear more than once in an extended IS reachability TLV. If it is repeated, a receiver should ignore all copies.
sections.plainLanguage: This field reports which protection capabilities a link has. Receivers can use the advertised information when considering links for GMPLS paths.

sections.title: Switching Capability and Bandwidth
sections.content:
The Interface Switching Capability Descriptor sub-TLV has type 21. It identifies a switching capability and encoding, then gives eight maximum LSP bandwidth values, one for each priority from 0 to 7. Each bandwidth value is a 4-octet IEEE floating-point number measured in bytes per second.

Additional fields depend on the switching capability. Packet-switching capabilities include a minimum bandwidth and interface MTU; TDM includes a minimum bandwidth and a SONET/SDH mode value. L2SC and LSC have no additional capability-specific fields. A link may advertise more than one descriptor.
sections.plainLanguage: The descriptor tells a router what kind of switching an interface supports and how much bandwidth it can offer at each priority. Some switching types also report a minimum bandwidth or interface size.

sections.title: Shared Risk Link Groups
sections.content:
The GMPLS-SRLG TLV has type 138 and carries a System ID, pseudonode number, flags, link identifiers or IPv4 addresses, and a list of SRLG values. Each SRLG value is 4 octets. The TLV length is 16 plus 4 times the number of SRLG values.

The least significant flag bit says whether the interface is numbered; the other flag bits are reserved. The SRLG TLV may occur more than once in an IS-IS Link State PDU. An SRLG indicates that multiple links share a risk, which matters when selecting paths that should not depend on the same resource.
sections.plainLanguage: An SRLG list identifies links that may fail together because they share a resource. A path planner can use that information when comparing possible routes.

sections.title: Advertising Resources During Restart
sections.content:
A restarting router may not yet know which resources remain available, including resources reserved by LSPs preserved across the restart. Until it can determine the remaining bandwidth, the RFC recommends advertising zero unreserved bandwidth and a Traffic Engineering Default metric of 0xffffff. For LSC or FSC links, it also recommends advertising zero maximum LSP bandwidth.

After calculating its unreserved resources, the router should advertise the resulting values. Before a planned restart, it should advertise zero unreserved bandwidth to discourage new LSP setup through it. Neighbors continue to advertise the actual unreserved bandwidth on their links toward the restarting node.
sections.plainLanguage: A restarting router should avoid advertising capacity it has not yet checked. Once it knows which resources remain free, it can advertise those values again.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The GMPLS traffic-engineering TLVs are not used for shortest-path-first computation or normal IP routing, so these extensions do not directly change IP routes. However, changing the TLVs may affect the underlying optical or SONET/SDH transport network.

Mechanisms that protect IS-IS Link State PDUs or traffic-engineering TLVs, including IS-IS cryptographic authentication described in RFC 5304, can also protect the GMPLS traffic-engineering information.
sections.plainLanguage: These fields do not directly change ordinary IP routing, but false link information could affect the transport network. The RFC points to IS-IS authentication as a way to protect the advertisements.
